issues.legal_issue: Land cultivated on behalf of a minor child does not prevent a tenant from purchasing tenanted land when the relevant holdings, including that land if counted, remain within the ceiling limit.
material_facts: The tenant held 36 acres and 1 gunta as an owner.
The disputed land included 7 acres and 34 guntas belonging to the tenant’s minor son, which the tenant cultivated on the son’s behalf.
Even if the son’s land were treated as joint-family property and included in the tenant’s holding, the total was found to be 43 acres and 35 guntas, within the ceiling limit.
The tenant cultivated the land he sought to purchase as a tenant and was a deemed tenant on the tiller date.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was entitled to purchase the land cultivated by him as a tenant because his holding remained within the ceiling limit, even if the minor son’s land was included.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 requires consideration of land held as owner or tenant in determining the ceiling for purchase eligibility. The Court held that even on the assumption that the minor son’s land was includible as joint-family property, the tenant’s holding remained within the ceiling. Under section 32, the tenant was a deemed tenant on the tiller date and could purchase the tenanted land.

predicates.tenant_purchase_proceeding: A proceeding concerns a tenant’s eligibility to purchase land cultivated by the tenant.
predicates.deemed_tenant_on_relevant_tiller_date: The claimant cultivated the land as a tenant and qualified as a deemed tenant on the applicable tiller date.
predicates.holdings_with_son_land_within_ceiling: The claimant’s relevant holdings remain within the ceiling even if land belonging to a minor child and cultivated on the child’s behalf is included.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeking to purchase cultivated land was a deemed tenant on the relevant date and the relevant holdings remain within the ceiling even with the minor child’s land included, the tenant is entitled to purchase the tenanted land.

issues.legal_issue: Land allotted to a family member in a partition is excluded from a tenant’s holding when the partition is supported by oral evidence and corroborating, unchallenged entries in official land records.
material_facts: The tenant claimed that land had been allotted to his brother in a partition.
The brother’s evidence supported the occurrence of a partition, although he could not give its date or year and no partition deed was produced.
Entries in the Record of Rights supported the claimed partition, were maintained in the ordinary course of official business, and their correctness was not challenged.
The lower tribunals relied on cultivation entries and the absence of a partition document but did not address the Record of Rights entries.
issues.conclusion: The land allotted to the brother in the partition had to be excluded from the tenant’s holding.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a partition need not be effected by a registered partition deed; a family arrangement can establish separate shares and their enjoyment. Entries in the Record of Rights, maintained in the official course of business and not challenged, are relevant documentary evidence that can corroborate oral evidence of partition and lend assurance to its acceptance.

rule.if: tenancy_ceiling_proceeding and land_claimed_as_allotted_by_family_partition and oral_evidence_supports_partition and official_land_records_support_partition and record_correctness_unchallenged

predicates.tenancy_ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding determines a tenant’s holding for the purpose of a ceiling limit affecting a land purchase.
predicates.land_claimed_as_allotted_by_family_parti: A claimant asserts that the land was allotted to another family member in a partition.
predicates.oral_evidence_supports_partition: A witness gives oral evidence supporting the occurrence of the partition.
predicates.official_land_records_support_partition: Entries made in official land records support the asserted partition.
predicates.record_correctness_unchallenged: No party challenges the correctness of the relevant official land-record entries.

issues.definition: In a tenancy ceiling proceeding, land claimed as allotted to a family member in a partition is excluded from the claimant’s holding when oral evidence and unchallenged official land-record entries support the partition.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may consider relevant evidence of partition that the tribunals below failed to address when reviewing their findings in a tenancy ceiling dispute.
material_facts: The tribunals below found that the tenant held land beyond the ceiling but did not address entries in the Record of Rights supporting the claimed partition.
The High Court considered those entries together with oral evidence of the partition.
The Supreme Court held that the entries were relevant evidence and that the High Court had rightly taken them into account.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to consider the Record of Rights entries when reviewing the tribunals’ findings.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that entries in official land records supporting a partition were relevant documentary evidence corroborating oral testimony. Because the tribunals below had not addressed those entries or the fact of partition, the High Court was right to consider that evidence in its review under Article 227 of the Constitution.

predicates.article_227_review_in_tenancy_ceiling_pr: A reviewing court considers tribunal findings in a proceeding determining a tenant’s holding for a ceiling limit.
predicates.lower_tribunals_omitted_relevant_partiti: The tribunals below did not address evidence relevant to an asserted partition.
predicates.official_records_support_partition: Entries in official land records support the asserted partition.

issues.definition: When tribunals in a tenancy ceiling proceeding omit relevant evidence of partition supported by official records, a reviewing court may consider that evidence.
